theory.title: The Scores a Prompt and a Reply Cost
overview: A chat service reads a prompt of 100 tokens and then writes a reply of 50 tokens. The model has 2 heads, so every count below is per head. Keep the cache between runs: the prompt is read in one prefill run, and each reply token is added by one decode run.

prompt.p: How many scores does the whole session compute?

answer.p: The prefill runs the model on 100 tokens at once, which computes the whole $100 \times 100$ table, so 10,000 scores. The reply is then written one token at a time. The first decode run adds the 101st token and compares its query with the 101 keys now in the cache, the next with 102, and the 50th with 150:
The decode runs do not compute $101^2$, $102^2$ and so on. Only the new row of each run is new, and the rows computed by the prefill are already in the cache.

prompt.p: How many would it compute if every run started from scratch, with no cache kept between them?

answer.p: The prefill still costs 10,000, and each of the 50 decode runs computes a whole table, on 101 tokens, then 102, up to 150:

The sum of the squares is the sum up to 150 less the sum up to 100, which is $1{,}136{,}275 - 338{,}350 = 797{,}925$, so the session costs $10{,}000 + 797{,}925 = 807{,}925$. That is 49.6 times the cached count.

prompt.p: A colleague says the cache saves the same share of the work whatever the length of the reply. With the same 100-token prompt, the reply is cut to 20 tokens. Is the colleague right, and why?

answer.p: The colleague is wrong. With 20 reply tokens the cached count is $10{,}000 + (101 + \dots + 120) = 10{,}000 + 2{,}210 = 12{,}210$, and from scratch it is $10{,}000 + (101^2 + \dots + 120^2) = 10{,}000 + 244{,}870 = 254{,}870$, a ratio of 20.9 instead of 49.6.

The share that falls is the prefill's, since its 10,000 scores are the same whether the reply is 20 tokens or 200. Decode rows grow with the length of the text, so the longer the reply the more of the session is decode rows, and the more the cache saves: 174 times at 200 reply tokens. A short reply on a long prompt is the case where the cache saves least, because the prompt's one run dominates the count and a run from scratch on the prompt has to be done anyway.
